title: Services and Logs
lead: Manage services with systemd and systemctl, write a simple unit file, and find the cause of problems in the journal and in /var/log.
objectives: You check, start, stop and enable services with systemctl and know the difference between start and enable.
You know the service names on RHEL/Rocky and Debian/Ubuntu (sshd/ssh, httpd/apache2, firewalld/ufw).
You read a unit file ([Unit], [Service], [Install]) and create a custom unit with daemon-reload.
You read logs with journalctl and with classic files in /var/log, and you know logrotate and the persistent journal.

sections.title: systemd and systemctl
body: **systemd** is the first process (PID 1) of almost every modern distribution and manages **units**. The most common types are `service` (a daemon such as sshd), `target` (a group of units, like a run level) and `timer` (a scheduled job, modern cron alternative).

`systemctl` is the control tool. **start** runs a service **now**, **enable** only makes it start **at boot**. They are independent: a service can be running but disabled, or enabled but stopped. `enable --now` does both at once.

`reload` makes a service re-read its configuration without a restart (not every service supports it); `restart` stops and starts it. The state commands `status`, `is-active` and `is-enabled` only read and are always safe.
Changing a service needs root, so use `sudo`. All systemctl commands are real-VM only; the built-in terminal cannot run them, so in the simulator you only write the command down.

commands.why: After a reboot the service comes up again without you.

commands.example: systemctl is-active sshd && systemctl is-enabled sshd

sections.warn: Never run stop, disable or mask on a service you do not know. Stopping the wrong service can take a machine offline.
sections.danger: **Never stop, disable or mask sshd or the network service on a remote VM.** You cut your own connection and cannot reconnect. In this module only read ssh/cron/chronyd state.

sections.title: Service names on different distributions
body: The same software has different unit names on different families. On RHEL/Rocky/Alma the SSH service is `sshd`, on Debian/Ubuntu it is `ssh` (an alias `sshd` often works too). The web server is `httpd` on RHEL and `apache2` on Debian/Ubuntu. The firewall is `firewalld` on RHEL and `ufw` on Ubuntu.

The cron service is `crond` on RHEL and `cron` on Debian/Ubuntu; the time service is `chronyd` (RHEL) or `chrony`/`systemd-timesyncd` (Ubuntu). If a name is not found, search with `list-unit-files`. `/etc/os-release` tells you which family you are on.

commands.what: Shows the distribution name and version.
commands.where: Before you use a service or log name.
commands.why: ID and ID_LIKE tell you whether you are on the RHEL or the Debian family.

commands.what: Lists the currently loaded services with their state.
commands.where: When you want to know what runs on the machine.
commands.why: You see real names instead of guessing.

commands.what: Lists all installed unit files with their boot setting.
commands.where: When a name is unknown or a service is not loaded yet.
commands.why: Also finds stopped and disabled services.

commands.what: Lists timer units with next and last run.
commands.where: When looking for scheduled jobs of systemd.
commands.why: Timers replace many cron jobs.

sections.tip: Names that are common on one family may not exist on the other. Use `ssh` or `sshd` with tab completion: `systemctl status ssh<TAB>`.

sections.title: Unit files and a custom service
body: A service is described in a **unit file** with three parts. `[Unit]` has the description and ordering, `[Service]` says what is run (`ExecStart=` with the **full path**) and how (`Restart=on-failure` restarts it after a crash), `[Install]` says where it is hooked in when enabled (`WantedBy=multi-user.target`).
Packages place their units in `/usr/lib/systemd/system` (on Debian also `/lib/systemd/system`). **Do not edit those.** Your own units and overrides go to `/etc/systemd/system`, which has priority.
After every new or changed unit file run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, so systemd re-reads the files. Without it you get a warning or the old version keeps running. Minimal example:

`[Unit]` `Description=Linux Lab demo` — `[Service]` `ExecStart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600` `Restart=on-failure` — `[Install]` `WantedBy=multi-user.target`. The VM exercises build exactly this unit as `linux-lab-demo.service` and remove it again.

commands.what: Prints the unit file including drop-in overrides.
commands.where: When you want to see what a service really runs.
commands.why: Shows ExecStart and the file path without searching.

commands.what: Creates a drop-in override in /etc/systemd/system without touching the original.
commands.where: When changing a packaged service.
commands.why: Survives package updates; daemon-reload happens automatically.

commands.what: Checks a unit file for syntax errors.
commands.where: Before you start a new unit.
commands.why: Finds typos like Exec_Start or a relative path.

commands.what: Lists units by the time they needed during boot.
commands.where: When the boot is slow.
commands.why: Shows the slowest units at the top.

sections.tip: Typical unit errors: `ExecStart=sleep 3600` (relative path, needs `/usr/bin/sleep`), a typo in a key name, a missing `[Install]` (then `enable` says there is no installation config).
sections.warn: Do not copy unit files into /usr/lib/systemd/system and do not delete units of the system. Work only with your own `linux-lab-demo.service` in /etc/systemd/system.

sections.title: journalctl and the kernel log
body: systemd collects all messages in the **journal**. `journalctl` reads it. Combine filters: `-u` for a unit, `-b` for the current boot, `-p err` for the priority error and worse, `--since` for time, `-n 50` for the last 50 lines, `-f` to follow live (end with Ctrl+C).
`journalctl -xe` jumps to the end with extra explanations; it is what systemctl suggests after a failed start. In scripts and when pasting output use `--no-pager`.

By default the journal may be kept only in memory (`/run/log/journal`) and is lost at reboot. For a **persistent journal** create `/var/log/journal` (or set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`) and restart journald. On Ubuntu it is persistent already; on many RHEL systems it is not.
`journalctl --disk-usage` shows how much space the journal uses. `dmesg` prints the kernel ring buffer (hardware, drivers, disk errors); on some systems it needs `sudo`.

commands.what: Follows new log lines live.

commands.why: You see the reaction immediately; leave with Ctrl+C.

commands.where: After a reboot or crash.
commands.why: Cuts out old noise.

commands.what: Filters by priority: err and everything worse.
commands.where: For a quick list of real problems.
commands.why: Hides info and debug messages.

commands.what: Shows entries from a point in time (`--until` for the end).
commands.where: When you know roughly when it happened.
commands.why: Keeps output small.

commands.where: For quick checks and for pasting into tickets.
commands.why: No scrolling in less, easy to copy.

commands.what: Opens the end of the journal with explanations.
commands.where: Right after a failed start.
commands.why: systemd itself suggests it in the error message.

commands.where: When /var fills up.

commands.why: Frees space, but the old logs are gone for good.

commands.what: Prints the kernel messages.
commands.where: For disk, USB, network card or memory problems.

sections.tip: Combine filters: `journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager`.
sections.warn: `--vacuum-time` and `--vacuum-size` delete logs permanently. Do not run them on a VM whose logs you still need for an investigation.

sections.title: Classic log files, rsyslog and logrotate
body: Besides the journal there are text logs in `/var/log`, written mostly by **rsyslog**. The names differ: on RHEL/Rocky `/var/log/messages` (general) and `/var/log/secure` (login and sudo); on Debian/Ubuntu `/var/log/syslog` and `/var/log/auth.log`. These files are readable only by root or the `adm` group, so use `sudo`.
Typical tools: `tail -f` follows a file, `grep -i error` searches it, `less` scrolls through it (`/word` searches, `q` quits). Combine them: `sudo grep -i error /var/log/messages | tail -n 20`.

**logrotate** keeps logs from growing forever: it renames, compresses and deletes old files by rules in `/etc/logrotate.conf` and `/etc/logrotate.d/`. A rule has the log path and options like `weekly`, `rotate 4` (keep 4 old copies), `compress`, `missingok`, `notifempty`. It is started daily by a timer or cron.
The simulator has the files of a RHEL machine, so you can practise reading logs here.

commands.what: Lists the log files and folders.
commands.where: To find out which logs exist.
commands.why: File names differ by distribution.

commands.what: Reads a log that only root may read (Ubuntu: `/var/log/auth.log`).
commands.where: When you investigate logins and sudo.
commands.why: Shows who logged in and who failed.

commands.what: Shows the end of a file and follows new lines.
commands.where: While a service is running or being tested.
commands.why: Live view; leave with Ctrl+C.

commands.what: Searches lines case-insensitively; `-c` counts them.
commands.where: To find errors in a big log.
commands.why: Reduces thousands of lines to the relevant ones.

commands.what: Shows a file page by page; `/word` searches, `q` quits.
commands.where: For long logs.
commands.why: Scrolling without flooding the terminal.

commands.what: Debug mode: shows what logrotate would do without doing it.
commands.where: After writing a new rule in /etc/logrotate.d.
commands.why: Tests the rule safely.

sections.tip: To count the errors: `grep -ci error /var/log/messages`. To see only the last lines of a long search: add `| tail -n 5`.
sections.warn: Never delete or truncate a log file with `rm` or `> file` while a service writes to it; let logrotate do it. Deleting evidence also makes later troubleshooting impossible.

t01.text: List the log files of the machine with `ls /var/log`.

t02.text: You cannot run systemctl here, so write the command you would use on a VM to show the state of sshd into a file: `echo "systemctl status sshd" > ~/answer_status.txt`.
t02.hint: The file is checked for `systemctl status sshd` (or `ssh`).

t03.text: Find the error lines in the general log with `grep -i error /var/log/messages`.
t03.hint: `-i` ignores upper/lower case, so ERROR is found too.

t04.text: Count how many lines contain `error` (ignore case) with `grep -ci error /var/log/messages`.
t04.hint: `-c` prints the number instead of the lines.

t05.text: Read the login log, which only root may read: `sudo cat /var/log/secure`.
t05.hint: Without sudo you get Permission denied; `student` is in the wheel group.

t06.text: The file `~/lab/systemctl_status.txt` is saved output of `systemctl status`. Show its `Loaded` line with `grep Loaded ~/lab/systemctl_status.txt`. Is the service enabled?
t06.hint: In the `Loaded:` line look for `enabled` or `disabled`.

t07.text: `~/lab/failed_units.txt` is a saved `systemctl list-units --failed`. Write only the unit names into `~/lab/failed_names.txt`: `cut -d" " -f1 ~/lab/failed_units.txt | grep service > ~/lab/failed_names.txt`.
t07.hint: `cut -d" " -f1` takes the first column, `grep service` drops the header and the summary line.

t08.text: Write the journalctl command for the last 50 lines of the sshd log without pager into `~/answer_journal.txt`, e.g. `echo 'journalctl -u sshd -n 50 --no-pager' > ~/answer_journal.txt`.

t09.text: `~/lab/logrotate_demo.conf` is a logrotate rule. Show the `rotate` line with `grep rotate ~/lab/logrotate_demo.conf`. How many old copies are kept?
t09.hint: `rotate 4` means four old copies; `weekly` means a weekly rotation.

t10.text: Predict: which messages are the last two lines of `/var/log/messages`? Guess first, then check with `tail -n 2 /var/log/messages`.
t10.hint: `tail -n 2` prints the last two lines; the newest entry is at the bottom.

t11.text: Predict: how many lines of `~/lab/journal_sample.txt` contain the word `Failed` (case-sensitive, so FAILURE does not count)? Guess first, then verify with `grep -c Failed ~/lab/journal_sample.txt`.
t11.hint: Read the file first with `cat ~/lab/journal_sample.txt` if you want to count by eye.

t12.text: Predict: who owns `/var/log/secure` and who may read it? Check with `ls -l /var/log/secure`.
t12.hint: Mode `-rw-------` means only the owner (root) can read and write.

t13.text: Debug: `~/lab/broken1.service` would not start, because the key is misspelled and the command has no full path. Rewrite the file (for example with `printf` and `>`) so that it has `ExecStart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600`.
t13.hint: `cat ~/lab/broken1.service` shows the error; the key must be `ExecStart`, the path `/usr/bin/sleep`.

t14.text: Debug: `systemctl enable` would complain about `~/lab/broken2.service` because it has no `[Install]` section. Append `[Install]` and `WantedBy=multi-user.target` with `printf` and `>>`.

t15.text: Mini project: create `~/lab/linux-lab-demo.service` with `[Unit]` (Description), `[Service]` (`ExecStart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600`) and `[Install]` (`WantedBy=multi-user.target`). Then write the three VM steps (copy to `/etc/systemd/system/`, `daemon-reload`, `enable --now linux-lab-demo.service`) into `~/lab/install_steps.txt`, one per line.
t15.hint: Use `printf` with `\n` for line breaks. The steps file only contains text; nothing is installed.

t16.text: Challenge: build an incident report `~/lab/incident.txt`. First write all error lines of `/var/log/messages` (case-insensitive) into it, then append the content of `/var/log/secure`. The report needs at least 4 lines.
t16.hint: `grep -i error ... > file`, then `sudo cat ... >> file` (the redirect is done by your own shell, so the file in your home is fine).

t17.text: TICKET #5610 — A customer reports that the web server does not come up after a reboot. Write the three commands you would run on a RHEL VM into `~/ticket_5610.txt`, one per line: show the state (`systemctl status httpd`), read its log (`journalctl -u httpd -n 50 --no-pager`) and enable and start it (`sudo systemctl enable --now httpd`).
t17.hint: Use one `printf` with `\n` between the lines. On Ubuntu the name would be `apache2`.

vm.intro: These tasks run on your own VM. Most are read-only. Task 4 creates a harmless unit that runs `sleep 3600`. **Take a snapshot first** and never stop or change sshd or the network service on a remote VM. Use `sshd`, `crond`, `chronyd` on RHEL/Rocky and `ssh`, `cron`, `chrony` on Ubuntu.

v01.title: Read service state
v01.text: Check ssh, cron and your time service without changing anything. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
# Rocky/RHEL
systemctl status sshd --no-pager
systemctl is-active crond chronyd
systemctl is-enabled sshd
# Ubuntu
systemctl status ssh --no-pager
systemctl is-active cron
systemctl is-enabled ssh
blocks.expected:
● sshd.service - OpenSSH server daemon
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service; enabled; ...)
     Active: active (running) since ...
active
active
enabled

differs: `Unit sshd.service could not be found` on Ubuntu: use `ssh` instead of `sshd`.
If `chronyd` is not found, your system uses `systemd-timesyncd` (Ubuntu); try `systemctl status systemd-timesyncd`.
Failed units in the list are not an error of this exercise; just note them.

v02.title: Read the journal
v02.text: Read the journal with filters and check how much space it uses. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
journalctl -b -n 10 --no-pager
journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | tail -n 5
journalctl --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager | wc -l
journalctl --disk-usage
blocks.expected:
... linux-lab systemd[1]: Started ...
1234
Archived and active journals take up 48.0M in the file system.

differs: `Permission denied` or a hint about the `systemd-journal` group: run the commands with `sudo`.
`-- No entries --` for `-p err` is good news: there were no errors.
If the journal only has the current boot, it is not persistent yet (see `ls /var/log/journal`).

v03.title: Classic logs and dmesg
v03.text: Read the end of the general and the login log, then the kernel log. Use the file names of your family.

blocks.cmd:
# Rocky/RHEL
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/messages
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/secure
# Ubuntu
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/syslog
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/auth.log
# both
sudo dmesg | tail -n 5
ls /etc/logrotate.d
blocks.expected:
Nov 12 10:01:02 linux-lab systemd[1]: ...
Nov 12 10:02:11 linux-lab sudo[2101]: student : TTY=pts/0 ; ...
[ 12.345678] ...

differs: `No such file or directory` for syslog/messages: the other family's file name, or rsyslog is not installed. The journal has the same data.
On Ubuntu, `dmesg` without sudo may be blocked; use `sudo dmesg`.

v04.title: Create your own service
v04.text: Create `linux-lab-demo.service`, load it, start it and look at its state and log. **Snapshot first.** The unit only runs `sleep 3600`.

blocks.cmd:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Linux Lab demo

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sleep 3600
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start linux-lab-demo.service
systemctl status linux-lab-demo.service --no-pager
systemctl is-enabled linux-lab-demo.service
journalctl -u linux-lab-demo.service -n 5 --no-pager
blocks.expected:
● linux-lab-demo.service - Linux Lab demo
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service; disabled; ...)
     Active: active (running) since ...
disabled
... systemd[1]: Started Linux Lab demo.

differs: `Failed to start ... No such file or directory`: check the path with `which sleep`; on some systems it is `/bin/sleep`.
`is-enabled` says `disabled` because you used start only; that is the difference between start and enable.
If `sudo` is missing the heredoc, copy the file in two steps: write it in your home and `sudo cp` it to /etc/systemd/system/.

v05.title: Remove your service again
v05.text: Stop and remove only `linux-lab-demo.service`, then check that systemd no longer knows it. Do not touch any other unit.

blocks.cmd:
sudo systemctl stop linux-lab-demo.service
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl status linux-lab-demo.service --no-pager
blocks.expected: Unit linux-lab-demo.service could not be found.

differs: If you also ran `enable`, run `sudo systemctl disable linux-lab-demo.service` before the `rm`.
`Unit ... not found` or `inactive (dead)` both mean the service is gone or not running.
Check the file name in `rm` twice: it must be exactly the demo file.

q1.q: What is the difference between `systemctl start` and `systemctl enable`?
options: start runs it now, enable makes it start at boot
enable runs it now, start makes it start at boot
start installs the package, enable removes it
q1.explain: start acts now, enable only changes the boot setting. `enable --now` does both.

q2.q: Which pair is the web server service on (RHEL, Ubuntu)?
q2.explain: RHEL/Rocky use `httpd`, Debian/Ubuntu use `apache2`. The same applies to sshd/ssh and firewalld/ufw.

q3.q: Which command shows only errors of the current boot?
q3.explain: `-b` limits to the current boot, `-p err` to priority error and worse.

q4.q: You created /etc/systemd/system/linux-lab-demo.service. What do you do first?
q4.explain: daemon-reload makes systemd read the new or changed unit file.

summary: `start`/`stop` act now, `enable`/`disable` act at boot, `enable --now` does both.
Names differ: sshd/ssh, httpd/apache2, firewalld/ufw, crond/cron; check with `/etc/os-release`.
A unit has `[Unit]`, `[Service]` (`ExecStart` with full path, `Restart=`), `[Install]`; own units go to `/etc/systemd/system` followed by `daemon-reload`.
`journalctl -u`, `-b`, `-p err`, `--since`, `-n 50 --no-pager`, `-f`, `-xe` find the cause; `--disk-usage` shows the size.
Classic logs: RHEL `messages`/`secure`, Debian/Ubuntu `syslog`/`auth.log`; logrotate rotates them by `/etc/logrotate.d` rules.
Never stop sshd on a remote VM; never delete or vacuum logs you still need.

glossary.meaning: The init system (PID 1) that starts and supervises services.
An object managed by systemd: service, target, timer, mount and more.
A group of units that describes a system state, e.g. multi-user.target.
A unit that starts another unit on a schedule; alternative to cron.
Makes systemd re-read unit files after you changed them.
Links a unit to /dev/null so that it cannot be started.
systemd's binary log database, read with journalctl.
The classic syslog daemon that writes text logs to /var/log.
Tool that rotates, compresses and deletes old log files by rules.
